beats.words: If you're someone who works with multiple AI agents inside of a terminal at the same time, this video's for you.
beats.says: This is for people juggling several AI agents at once.
beats.picture: Three loose keys, tossed at odd angles in the middle of the cream board. Each key's square head (its bow) carries one provider mark: Claude, OpenAI, Gemini. The Claude key lands first, alone and centred; on 'multiple' it slides left and the OpenAI and Gemini keys drop in beside it on 'AI' and 'agents'. On 'same time' all three jangle once (a single small swing) and settle, still loose and crooked.
beats.whiteboard_version: The marker draws the three crooked keys one after another, the first one centred, each mark stamped into its key's head as the key is drawn; on 'same time' three short marker ticks beside the keys show the jangle, then nothing moves.

beats.words: By using Warp, you can centralize all of the different providers that you're using inside of one simple application,
beats.says: Warp puts every provider you use into one application.
beats.picture: On 'Warp' a wall key rack draws above the loose keys: a long plank with two screws, the Warp mark and the word WARP on its face. On 'centralize' three J-hooks draw under the plank, and on 'all', 'different' and 'providers' each loose key flies up, straightens and hangs on its own hook with one small swing. PROVIDERS is written under the three hanging keys. On 'one simple application' the plank's own outline flips terracotta.

emphasis.why: The plank is a DRAWN object, so LAW 38 rule 2 applies: the plank's own outline stroke tweens from ink to terracotta (the board lane's panel border flip) on 'one' (9.62) and back at 11.00. Never a ring, never a highlight; there is no raster text in this video.

beats.whiteboard_version: Same picture: the plank and WARP are written first as the only type, the hooks are three short strokes, and each key is redrawn hanging (the crooked key is erased in the same instant its straight twin is inked on the hook, so each key only ever exists once).

beats.words: giving you access to everything that you might need in a nicer interface.
beats.says: One place gives you access to everything you need, and it is nicer to use.
beats.picture: The full rack holds still. On 'everything' the three key heads' outlines flip terracotta together, the keys you now have in one place; they return to ink at 13.70, before 'nicer interface' finishes.

emphasis.why: Each key head is a DRAWN object: its own outline stroke flips to terracotta (LAW 38 rule 2, border flip, no added geometry). The marks inside are rasters and are never boxed.

beats.whiteboard_version: The marker retraces the three key heads in terracotta on 'everything'.

beats.words: On top of this, they literally just released a new feature that allows you to use your Grok subscription with the Warp agent.
beats.says: New: your Grok subscription now works with Warp's agent.
beats.picture: On 'released' the three hanging keys, their hooks and PROVIDERS slide left together along the plank to make room. On 'new feature' a fourth J-hook draws at the right end of the plank. On 'Grok' a fourth key, with the Grok mark in its head, drops onto the new hook, swings once and settles; GROK is written under it on the same baseline as PROVIDERS. On 'subscription' the Grok key's head flips terracotta, and on 'Warp agent' the plank's outline flips terracotta with it, the new key now part of Warp.

bespoke_objects.name: three loose keys
bespoke_objects.why_bespoke: The hook object (LAW 20): three separate crooked keys, each with a provider's mark in its head, argue 'many separate AI agents to juggle' in one picture; a row of logo tiles would be furniture and says nothing about being scattered.
bespoke_objects.how_drawn: Each key is a rounded-square head (card fill, 7 px ink outline, the provider mark inside at 0.58 of the head) over a small ring loop, then a straight shaft with a groove line, three stepped teeth on the right and a pointed tip; the three sit at -18, +5 and +16 degrees at slightly different heights.

bespoke_objects.name: wall key rack
bespoke_objects.why_bespoke: The payoff object (LAW 13): Warp as the one plank every provider key hangs on is 'centralize all your providers in one application' as an everyday object, and it can take a new key later, which is exactly the Grok news.
bespoke_objects.how_drawn: A long rounded plank (card fill, 8 px ink outline) with two screw heads at its ends and the Warp mark plus WARP on its face, three J-hooks under it, and the three keys hanging straight from the hooks.

labels.note: LAW 9 key term: the FIRST type on the board, alone, 48 px (25.6 design units), written INSIDE the plank's face to the right of the Warp mark, like the word on a real key-rack sign, so it is the plank's own content (LAW 39: a key CONTAINED by its shape is that shape's content, never a label beside it). Spoken 5.62-5.86. Declare data-label-for="key-rack" in the DOM and label_plan= on the board.

LAW 39: centred under the three hanging keys' group axis (the middle key's axis), entirely below the key tips. Spoken 7.74-8.14. Travels with the three keys on the slide at 16.84 (LAW 28, one block). Declare data-label-for="key-openai" (the host it is centred under).

LAW 39 + LAW 50: entirely below the Grok key, centred on its axis, on the SAME baseline and in the same size as PROVIDERS, so the two sibling labels sit the same way. Spoken 19.42-19.64. data-label-for="key-grok".

boards.why: LAW 43's exception, chosen on purpose: the whole script is ONE accumulating object. The loose keys of the hook are the same keys that get hung on the rack, and the Grok news is one more key on that same rack; the finished frame (a Warp rack holding Claude, OpenAI, Gemini and Grok keys) IS the argument. An erase anywhere would cut the keys away from the rack they are about to hang on.

chapters.why_together: One idea that accumulates: separate keys, then one rack that holds them all, then one more key on it.

In the DOM lanes the keys slide left at 16.84 to make room for the fourth hook (LAW 19's sanctioned displacement). The whiteboard may do the same as an erase-and-redraw of the three hung keys one step left (an erase to free a column is legal), so both boards start centred and end centred.
